subsection: 6. The suffrage movement and educational reforms

notes.h: Women’s rights and the early suffrage societies (1870–1900)
notes.b: Suffrage means the right to vote. In Ireland the campaign for women’s suffrage began as a small, respectable effort among middle-class Protestant and Quaker women, closely linked to property rights, education and local government. It rested on feminism (the belief in women’s equal rights and public roles) and on the democratic argument that government by elected representatives was incomplete if half the adults had no say.
points: In 1870 Irish women had no parliamentary vote, and under common law a married woman’s property passed to her husband, so the law clearly favoured men. This is the grievance the early campaigners set out to change.

The Married Women’s Property Acts of 1870 and 1882 improved the position of married women, and the 1882 Act applied to Ireland as well as to England and Wales. Isabella Tod campaigned for these reforms.

Isabella Tod organised a suffrage society in Belfast in the early 1870s (1872 if a single year is wanted), the first in Ulster. This made Belfast the starting point of organised suffrage activity in the north.

Anna Haslam, a Quaker, and her husband Thomas Haslam founded the Dublin Women’s Suffrage Association in 1876, which later became the Irish Women’s Suffrage and Local Government Association. Anna Haslam (1829–1922) lived long enough to see women gain the vote in 1918.

The early societies used polite, constitutional methods: they petitioned MPs, held drawing-room meetings and sent speakers out. They also worked alongside the campaign for girls’ education and the campaign against the Contagious Diseases Acts.
Women also gained a role in local government, a stepping stone to the parliamentary vote.

The Local Government (Ireland) Act of 1898 let women vote in county and district council elections. They could also stand for district councils and boards of guardians (the bodies that ran poor relief), though not for county councils.

County and borough councils were only opened to women by an Act of 1911. So by 1898 women could vote locally and hold some local office, but the higher councils stayed closed to them for another thirteen years.

Several prominent Irish suffragists, such as Tod, were unionists, while others supported Home Rule (self-government for Ireland within the United Kingdom). The societies therefore stayed neutral on Home Rule for decades, because taking sides would have split their membership.
notes.tip: Examiners reward naming founders with years: Haslam and the Dublin society in 1876, and the Local Government Act of 1898 as the key local government date. Do not give 1887 or 1896 for local office. Say only that women gained local votes and office, with 1898 as the key date.

notes.b: Isabella Tod was a Belfast Presbyterian reformer who campaigned for women’s education, property rights and votes, always from a unionist outlook. She is the best example of the respectable, constitutional phase of the movement.
points: Isabella Tod (1836–1896) was born in Edinburgh, settled in Belfast and lived there until her death. She was a Presbyterian, which set her apart from the Catholic nationalist background of Hanna Sheehy-Skeffington.
She organised the first suffrage society in Ulster, in Belfast in the early 1870s. This was the earliest sustained women’s suffrage organisation in the north.
She was a participant in the campaigns that led to the Married Women’s Property Act of 1882, which gave married women more control over their own property.
On girls’ education she helped found the Ladies’ Institute in Belfast (1867), a society for girls’ education, and worked with Margaret Byers of the Ladies’ Collegiate School (later Victoria College).
She helped win the inclusion of girls in the Intermediate Education Act (1878) and the opening of Royal University degrees to women (1882), so she shaped both school and university access for girls.
She co-founded the Belfast Women’s Temperance Association in 1874 and campaigned against the Contagious Diseases Acts, so her reform interests went well beyond the vote.
As a Liberal Unionist she opposed Home Rule in 1886 and urged women to oppose it. She helped found the Irish Women’s Liberal Unionist Association.
Contemporaries respected her as a public speaker and organiser, though her unionism limited her influence among nationalists, who made up most of the Irish suffrage movement outside Ulster.
Historians present her as a pioneer who created the first sustained suffrage organisation in Ulster and helped break the exclusion of women from Irish public debate.
notes.tip: For a short paragraph on Tod, give birth (Edinburgh, 1836), where she worked (Belfast), the organisations she founded or joined, her causes (property, education, votes), her unionism and one assessment. Each correct, dated and relevant statement earns marks. Do not confuse her with Margaret Byers or Margaret Cousins.

notes.h: Suffrage organisations and the Irish Party (1900–1912)
notes.b: After 1900 the suffrage groups multiplied and divided into peaceful and radical wings. They found the main obstacle at Westminster, where the Irish Party (the nationalist party led by John Redmond) refused to back votes for women.
points: The Irish Women’s Suffrage Federation, founded in 1911 by Louie Bennett and others, linked local societies and used peaceful methods. Its members were suffragists, meaning peaceful, constitutional campaigners for the vote.
The Irish Women’s Franchise League (founded 1908) was more radical. It argued that no Home Rule settlement was legitimate without votes for women.
A Conciliation Bill proposing a limited vote for women was defeated in the House of Commons in March 1912, with most Irish Party members voting against it.

Redmond and his leading colleague John Dillon opposed the bill because they feared a franchise bill would complicate the passage of Home Rule, the Irish Party’s main aim. Redmond also personally opposed votes for women.

The Third Home Rule Bill of 1912 was the main political issue of the day, and unionists were resisting it. Suffragists therefore demanded that women’s votes be part of any Home Rule settlement, and argued that Home Rule without them would be incomplete.

Suffragists generally split on the national question. Some, like Hanna Sheehy-Skeffington, argued that independence would be incomplete without women’s votes, while others, notably in Ulster, were unionists.
notes.tip: Keep the two organisations apart: the Federation (1911) was peaceful and the Franchise League (1908) was militant. Explain the Irish Party’s opposition as fear for Home Rule: Redmond and Dillon did not want anything to complicate it.

notes.h: The Irish Women’s Franchise League, the Irish Citizen and militancy (1908–1914)
notes.b: From 1908 the Franchise League brought direct action to Irish politics, and its campaign peaked in 1912–13. Its members were suffragettes: militant campaigners for the vote who used direct action such as window-breaking. The word was coined by the British press.
points: The League was founded in Dublin in 1908 by Hanna Sheehy-Skeffington, Margaret Cousins, her husband James Cousins and Francis Sheehy-Skeffington. Its aim was votes for women on the same terms as men.

The League published a weekly newspaper, the Irish Citizen, from May 1912. It was edited at first by Francis Sheehy-Skeffington and James Cousins, and it ran until 1920, giving the movement a voice of its own.
In June 1912 eight League members, including Hanna Sheehy-Skeffington and Margaret Cousins, were arrested for breaking windows at government buildings in Dublin, and were imprisoned.

In July 1912 Asquith, the British Prime Minister, visited Dublin. English suffragettes of the Women’s Social and Political Union (WSPU) disrupted the visit, and Mary Leigh threw a hatchet at the carriage carrying Asquith and Redmond.
Imprisoned suffragettes went on hunger strike (refusing food as a protest). The English prisoners were force-fed in Mountjoy, the Dublin prison, which provoked public protest.

Hanna Sheehy-Skeffington was jailed again in 1913 and released after a hunger strike under the Cat and Mouse Act (1913), which let the authorities free weakened hunger strikers and re-arrest them later.

Hostile crowds attacked suffragettes at public meetings. Many nationalists and trade unionists considered the militant tactics counter-productive, because they thought the tactics turned opinion against the cause.
notes.tip: Separate the methods in your answer: constitutional societies from the 1870s to 1900s, then militancy from 1912. Remember that the English prisoners were force-fed, not Irish ones, and that the WSPU was English, not the League. Hanna’s part in 1912 was her own arrest, not organising the window-breaking.

notes.b: Hanna Sheehy-Skeffington was the leading Irish militant suffragist. She tied women’s rights to nationalism and socialism, and she was critical of the movements that put women second.
points: Hanna Sheehy-Skeffington (1877–1946) was born in Kanturk, Co. Cork, the daughter of the nationalist MP David Sheehy. She took an MA from the Royal University in 1902.
She married the pacifist and feminist Francis Skeffington in 1903, and they each added the other’s surname, a sign of their belief in equality in marriage.

She co-founded the Irish Women’s Franchise League in 1908, was imprisoned for window-breaking in 1912 and again in 1913 (with a hunger strike), and was a contributor and later editor of the Irish Citizen.

She was a participant in the campaign, and her organisation shaped how the issue was seen in Ireland. She was also a critic of the Irish Party and later of Cumann na mBan, which she saw as subordinating women to men.
Her husband Francis was shot without trial by Captain Bowen-Colthurst in April 1916, after this topic’s dates. She campaigned for an inquiry and refused compensation.
Contemporaries admired her courage, but many nationalists thought her tactics divisive, and unionists and the Irish Party saw her as a nuisance.
Historians now see her as a key figure of Irish feminism who insisted that independence must include equality.
notes.tip: For a short paragraph on Hanna, give birth (Kanturk, 1877), the League (1908), imprisonment (1912 and 1913), her causes, her nationalist outlook and one assessment. Do not mix her up with her husband Francis, who was the one shot in 1916.

notes.b: The suffrage cause was entangled with the national question (whether Ireland should have Home Rule or stay fully in the Union), and women in each camp chose their side. This division was one of the movement’s main weaknesses.
points: Unionist women in Ulster signed their own declaration against Home Rule on Ulster Day, 28 September 1912, about 234,000 of them. This gave them a public role in unionism, and suffragists such as Tod had been unionists.

Nationalist women formed Cumann na mBan in April 1914 to support the Irish Volunteers. Suffragists such as Sheehy-Skeffington objected to its auxiliary status, meaning it served the men’s organisation rather than acting on its own.

Many suffragists argued that women should not be asked to postpone their claim until Home Rule or the Union had been settled, because the vote was a democratic right whatever the constitutional outcome.
The Irish Citizen pursued both aims, and it attracted writers from different political groups, from the pacifist movement to the trade unions.
Votes for women were granted in 1918 under the Representation of the People Act, to women over thirty with a property qualification (or married to a qualified man).
This came after the First World War, and the Irish Party that had opposed the cause had by then been destroyed, in the December 1918 election.
notes.tip: Examiners ask about suffrage as a controversy: the Irish Party’s fear for Home Rule, nationalist and unionist suspicion, and public hostility to militancy, set against the suffragists’ democratic argument. Use the dated examples, Ulster Day 1912 and Cumann na mBan 1914, to show the division.

notes.b: Before 1878 secondary schools were mostly private or run by religious orders, with little state funding. The Intermediate Education Act of 1878 began state support and used examinations to decide how much each school was paid; primary education was reformed later, in 1900.
points: The Intermediate Education (Ireland) Act (1878) set up an Intermediate Board that held public examinations (junior, middle and senior grades) for boys and girls from 1879.
Schools were paid results fees according to how many pupils passed, a system known as payment by results. Prizes and exhibitions (money awards) rewarded top candidates.
The system financed denominational schools (schools run by a particular church) without interfering in their management, so Catholic, Protestant and convent schools all grew.

Girls’ schools used the examinations to compete with boys, because the exams were open to girls too. Alexandra College (Dublin, 1866), Victoria College (Belfast) and the Loreto and Dominican convent schools all prepared girls.
Critics said payment by results encouraged cramming (learning facts just to pass), narrowed the curriculum to examinable subjects and neglected Irish and science.

National school (primary) teachers had been paid by results since the 1870s. The Revised Programme of 1900 ended this, broadening the curriculum to include drawing, practical work, nature study and Irish as an ordinary subject within school hours.
The bilingual programme of 1904 encouraged teaching through Irish in Gaeltacht (Irish-speaking) schools.
Victoria College in Belfast, founded by Margaret Byers in 1859 as the Ladies’ Collegiate School, and Alexandra College, founded in 1866, were pioneers of girls’ secondary education.
notes.tip: Be ready to say what the 1878 Act did, how payment by results worked, why it was criticised, and what the 1900 programme changed. Keep the dates apart: the Act of 1878 (secondary, exams from 1879) and the Revised Programme of 1900 (primary). For a short paragraph, include public examinations for boys and girls, results fees, the effect on denominational schools, criticism and the 1900 change.

notes.h: The Royal University and the Irish Universities Act (1879–1913)
notes.b: University education was a grievance for Catholics and a barrier for women. The Royal University opened degrees to both groups, and the Act of 1908 then settled the university question with two new universities.
points: Trinity College Dublin was Protestant in ethos, and the Catholic hierarchy (the bishops) banned Catholics from attending it. Catholics therefore complained that no university gave them a real Catholic institution.

The Royal University of Ireland (Act 1879, charter 1880) was an examining body that awarded degrees to students of any college or none. It replaced the Queen’s University as the examining and degree-awarding body.
Degrees were opened to women by a supplemental charter in 1882, and the first women graduated in the early 1880s. Hanna Sheehy-Skeffington was among its later graduates, taking her MA in 1902.

The Irish Universities Act (1908), prepared by Chief Secretary Augustine Birrell, dissolved the Royal University and created the National University of Ireland (NUI), with constituent colleges at Dublin, Cork and Galway, and Queen’s University Belfast.
The NUI had a Catholic ethos, which made it acceptable to Catholics, with Archbishop William Walsh of Dublin as first chancellor. It was open to women on equal terms.

The Gaelic League, the organisation promoting the Irish language, campaigned for compulsory Irish for matriculation (the entrance qualification). The NUI Senate decided in 1910 to require it, applied from 1913.
notes.tip: On universities, explain why the Catholic grievance existed (Trinity’s ethos and the bishops’ ban) and how 1908 answered it. Do not credit Tod with the Royal University charter: the Act was 1879, the charter 1880 and degrees opened to women in 1882.

notes.h: Assessment: the suffrage and education record
notes.b: Reforms opened up public life to women and widened access to education, but the parliamentary vote came late and by a different route. Judging the movement means weighing what it achieved against what it could not do.
points: Achievement: women gained the vote in local government elections and the right to hold local office, took degrees and entered the professions, and built an organised movement with its own newspaper.
Limit: Irish women had no parliamentary vote before 1918, the Home Rule Bills offered them none, and militancy gained little and divided opinion.
Achievement: the Intermediate system and the 1908 Act widened access to secondary and university education, especially for girls and Catholics.
Limit: payment by results encouraged cramming and a narrow curriculum, and denominational divisions over education persisted for decades.
Contemporary Irish Party leaders saw suffrage as a distraction from Home Rule, whereas suffragists saw the vote as a democratic right.
Historians stress that the movement was divided by the national question, which weakened it, but that its organisation gave women experience used in later politics.
notes.tip: Higher level essays reward a clear judgement stated at the start, then dated points: organisations, methods, opposition and results (local government 1898, vote 1918). Separate achievements from limits, and constitutional methods from militancy.
